query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, adherent oxide surface layer on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance during high‐temperature use without significantly compromising its inherent ductility and yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a high-temperature (≈1000 °C) yield strength of 163–530 MPa, but with poor oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Expose the as-cast alloy to a short-duration, high-temperature pre-oxidation process (e.g., 1–3 hours at ≈1000 °C in a controlled, low‐partial‐pressure oxygen atmosphere) to form a compact, protective oxide film on its surface.
generation.conditions: Pre-treatment at 1000 °C for 1–3 hours in an atmosphere with controlled oxygen partial pressure followed by subsequent high-temperature service (around 1000 °C) in air or oxygen-rich environments at strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous and adherent oxide layer (likely enriched in HfO2 and/or TiO2) that acts as an effective barrier to oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide barrier limits oxygen diffusion into the underlying bulk, thereby reducing subsequent oxidation damage during high-temperature exposure while preserving the bulk mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The intervention is expected to result in a lower rate of oxidation (i.e., reduced mass gain and oxide scale thickness) during high-temperature exposure, with mechanical test results (tensile ductility and yield strength) remaining comparable to the untreated cast alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers from rapid oxygen ingress at high temperatures, which deteriorates its mechanical performance, particularly under prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is predicted to be effective for high-temperature exposures up to about 1000 °C and for durations on the order of hours; performance under extreme cyclic thermal loading or much longer exposures is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, thickness, and long-term stability of the oxide layer under cyclic loading remain to be fully characterized, and potential impacts on fatigue behavior are not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens. Subject one set to the described pre-oxidation treatment (1–3 hours at 1000 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere) and leave the other set untreated. Then expose both sets to high-temperature service conditions (e.g., 1000 °C in air for 10 hours) and perform post-exposure mechanical testing.
measurements: Mass gain during high-temperature exposure via thermogravimetric analysis
Surface oxide layer characterization (using X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy)
High-temperature yield strength tests under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (lower mass gain and thinner, more adherent oxide layer) while maintaining tensile ductility and yield strength comparable to the untreated specimens, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.
